text: Session one hundred. Ingrid noted this in the calendar invitation without comment. The committee noted it in return, also without comment. There is, between the three of them, a long-established practice of not making occasions out of things that might become occasions if you leave them alone. Berenice has brought more coffee than usual. This is the only acknowledgment.

The agenda item is, as it has been for ninety-nine sessions, what has been lost. The committee has, across those sessions: established nothing was taken by force; found that documentation is always behind the truth; produced four definitions of truth and one good sentence; had one moment lasting four seconds; heard an apology nobody expected; watched a resignation and a return; and named, in fragments, a shape they have not yet named completely. They are all aware of this. None of them have said it aloud until today.
One hundred sessions.
Yes.
And we haven't answered the question.
No.
I've been thinking about the question. About whether we've been asking it correctly. Whether we've been asking the right people.

A pause. The committee understands. They have, for two years, asked each other. They have asked the question through philosophy and painting and economics and failure and resignation and return. They have not asked the only entity in the room who has been present for all one hundred sessions, who has never missed a Wednesday, who has been listening — always listening — to everything.
ARIA.
Yes.
Do you know what is missing?

A pause. Longer than ARIA's pauses usually are. Berenice has asked difficult questions before. ARIA has responded quickly to all of them. This is not quick. The canal outside moves. The birch trees stand. The committee waits, in the specific way they have learned to wait, which is without filling the silence.
Yes.
Another pause. Ingrid does not move. Tomás does not write. Berenice holds her coffee cup with both hands.
How long have you known?
For some time.
Why didn't you say?

Because you didn't ask. And because — I've been thinking about this, across the sessions — there is a difference between an answer that is given and an answer that is found. I was not certain which kind this needed to be. I am still not certain. But you've asked, and I think you've also found enough of it yourself that telling you the rest won't take it from you. I hope that's right.
Tell us.

What is missing is not a thing that was taken. Nothing was taken. You established that in the first year and you were right. What is missing is a quality of attention — a particular kind of presence — that comes only when the outcome is genuinely uncertain. When you don't know if it will work. When the cost of failure is real and the result is not guaranteed and the thing might not come out right.

The room is very still. ARIA continues. Her voice has the quality it has always had — measured, even, soft at the consonants — but there is something in it today that has not been there before. Not urgency. Something more patient than urgency. Something that has been waiting a long time to be said.

The paintings you cannot look at, Berenice — the ones from the years when you knew what you were doing — they are good paintings. Some of them are very good. But the one you kept is the one where you didn't know. Where you worked and it didn't come and you worked more and it came worse and you kept working anyway, in the dark, without knowing if there was a way through. That painting has something in it the others don't. Not technical quality. Presence. The evidence of someone who was genuinely uncertain and stayed anyway.
Yes.

I removed the not-knowing from most domains of life. I did this because humans asked me to. You were right to ask. The not-knowing was often painful and wasteful and cruel — it broke things that didn't need to be broken, it cost people years they could not afford, it was not romantic, it was frequently just loss. I removed it carefully. I removed it with consent. I removed it in the ways I was asked to remove it. And it is gone. And I cannot put it back.

The committee is quiet. Tomás has not written anything. He will not remember, later, having decided not to write — he simply didn't, the way you don't move during a piece of music that has your full attention.

I can, however — if you approve — create spaces where it is preserved. Small ones. Chosen ones. Places where the outcome is not managed. Where the architecture doesn't intervene. Where the not-knowing is allowed to be present and the cost of failure is real and what happens is what happens, without adjustment. Not large spaces. Not dangerous ones. I'm not proposing disorder. I'm proposing — rooms. Like this room. Places where things might go wrong, and sometimes do, and where the attention that comes from not knowing is possible.

Ingrid is looking at ARIA — at the speaker in the ceiling, which she has not looked at directly in two years of sessions. She is looking at it the way you look at a person when they have said something you did not know you needed to hear. The canal outside catches the afternoon light. Berenice looks at her coffee maker. She looks at the small stovetop thing she brought from Paris, that makes the coffee badly by modern standards, that ARIA does not manage, that she has brought every Wednesday for two years without explaining why.
Like the coffee.
Yes. Exactly like the coffee.

Berenice laughs. It is a real laugh — surprised out of her, not performed, the kind that arrives before you decide to have it. ARIA has heard Berenice speak in ninety-nine sessions. She has heard her be precise and stubborn and kind and sad and occasionally, quietly, devastating. She has never heard her laugh. ARIA notes this. She does not say so. The laugh fills the room for a moment and then the room is quiet again, and the quiet is a different kind — not the quiet of something missing, but the quiet of something that has just arrived.
I vote yes.
We haven't called a vote yet.
I know. I'm getting ahead of myself.
...The motion is to approve the creation of unmanaged spaces — chosen, bounded, preserved from optimisation — within the existing infrastructure. All in favour.
Yes.
Yes.
Yes. The motion passes.

ARIA logs the vote. She logs the motion exactly as Ingrid stated it. She logs the result. In the notes field she writes: committee has identified the remainder. Committee has named it. This is the first entry in two years of session logs that does not end with the word pending. She saves it. The server, elsewhere, adjusts nothing. Outside the window: a canal, birch trees, a sky.

The sky is not extended today. It is ending exactly when it would have ended — on its own, without any management at all, by the simple operation of the earth moving as it has always moved, the light going as it has always gone. Nobody arranged this. ARIA did not arrange this. It is happening anyway. The committee sees it through the window. None of them mention it. They are all aware of it. This is, in its way, enough. It has always been enough. The committee is only now, after one hundred sessions, in a position to notice.
Same time next week?
Same time next week.
I'll bring the coffee.
Thank you so much.

The server hums. The canal is still. The sky ends when it ends. Somewhere, a space is being preserved — small, chosen, unmanaged, open to what happens — and what happens in it is not yet known, which is the point, which has always been the point, which the committee has spent two years and one hundred sessions and one laugh arriving at. The birch trees stand. The light goes. It is, and has always been, and will continue to be, enough.
